hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: The volume spike may mark genuine information arrival (a repricing), so price continues down and the 'absorption' bounce never comes; alternatively the bounce is real but only a few basis points, which the 10bp round-trip cost erases. Also, the trigger is rare, so the sample may be too thin for the reversal edge to be distinguished from noise.
hypotheses.hypothesis: When an extreme volume print coincides with a sharp short-horizon drawdown, the flow is likely forced (stop cascades / liquidation engine market orders) rather than informed. Forced sellers must cross the spread at any price, pushing price beyond the level justified by information; passive liquidity providers who absorb the imbalance require compensation and are repaid as price snaps back once the queue of forced orders is exhausted. Entering long on a >2.5 sigma volume bar following a -0.4% 30-minute slide should capture that inventory-rebate over the following couple of hours.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Low-volatility trend regimes are exactly where drift per bar is smallest, so a 4-hour hold may produce less than 10bp net; and the persistence requirement delays entry so much that we buy the final leg before the volatility regime flips, converting a grind-up into a fast mean-reverting flush.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Slow, low-volatility uptrends are the signature of sustained one-sided passive accumulation (programmatic or mandate-driven buying that works orders patiently). In such regimes realised volatility stays compressed while price grinds above its moving average, and there is little liquidation-driven two-way churn to shake positioning out. Requiring the price to hold above its 8-hour SMA by >0.5% for six consecutive bars while 8-hour volatility stays below 0.15% per bar should isolate this accumulation regime, where drift over the next four hours exceeds the cost hurdle.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Clock effects of this kind are venue- and era-specific and are the first thing arbitrageurs remove; the residual drift is likely a fraction of a basis point per trade while the round trip costs 10bp. Also, taking every hour boundary generates a very high trade count, so cost accumulation should dominate any tiny directional edge.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Institutional and algorithmic execution schedules, index/perp basis hedging and periodic funding-related rebalancing cluster on round hour boundaries, producing a burst of same-direction taker flow at the top of the hour. If the 1-hour moving-average slope is already positive (negative) at the hour boundary, that clustered flow tends to extend the prevailing micro-drift for the next half hour. Trading the sign of ma_slope(12) only on bars that close the hour isolates a scheduled-flow mechanism rather than a price pattern.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Range expansion is frequently symmetric and terminal: the sweep exhausts the very stop liquidity that fuelled it, so entry lands at the top of the impulse and the two-hour hold gives back the move. Range and trend are also strongly correlated in a directional market, so the filter may add no information and the rule degenerates into buying strength after it has already happened.
hypotheses.hypothesis: When the 8-hour high-low range expands past ~1.2% of price while price simultaneously sits above its 8-hour average, the book has been swept through prior resting liquidity: stop clusters and breakout-chasing algorithms are triggered, and market makers widen and skew quotes rather than defend the old range. The resulting thin book means incremental buy flow moves price disproportionately, so directional continuation over the next two hours should exceed costs. The joint range-plus-trend condition distinguishes an upside expansion from a two-sided volatility blow-off.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Shorting strength during a high-volatility regime has an unbounded left tail: if the sweep is the start of a short squeeze, momentum continues and the fixed 30-minute hold realises a large loss that outweighs many small wins. The impact-decay component may also be smaller than 10bp, since it decays inside the first bar or two before the fill at the next open.
hypotheses.hypothesis: A vertical up-impulse (>0.3% in fifteen minutes) occurring while one-hour realised volatility is already elevated is typically a market-order sweep into a temporarily depleted ask side rather than a considered repricing. Micro-price overshoots the fair level by roughly the depth-weighted impact; once the aggressor stops, market makers refill and mean-revert their inventory, so the top few basis points of the spike are given back within half an hour. Shorting the impulse with a short 30-minute hold trades that impact-decay component.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Low volume is also the signature of a drifting, uncontested market that keeps drifting (holiday-style or off-peak grind), in which case the fade fights persistent drift. Additionally, volume z-score is regime-dependent and mean-reverting on its own, so the filter may simply select the tail of a volume lull with no reliable directional consequence, leaving costs as the only reliable term.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Price advances that occur on below-average volume reflect withdrawal of passive bid-side liquidity rather than genuine accumulation: the same notional of buy flow lifts price further when the book is thin, so the move carries little participation and no real position transfer. Such moves are structurally fragile because there is no accumulated long inventory to defend the level, and price retraces once normal two-way flow resumes. Requiring a +0.5% four-hour advance while four-hour volume z-score is below -0.5 isolates this participation divergence and should give a fade edge over the next two hours.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: The slow MA slope is autocorrelated but nearly zero-mean over multi-hour horizons, so signed forward returns average well under 10 bps; alternatively the slope flips inside the 48-bar hold and long/short legs cancel, leaving pure cost bleed of roughly -10 bps per trade.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Perpetual futures inherit slow directional drift from spot inventory and basis/funding pressure: when the 24-hour moving average itself is sloping, hedgers and trend-following allocators keep pushing the same direction for many hours. Prior failures all traded fast signals whose gross edge (~1 bp) could never clear 10 bps round-trip, so this proposal deliberately uses the slowest available feature (ma_slope over 288 bars) with a 4-hour hold so that each round trip spans a move large enough to amortise cost, and no other conditions so trade count stays low relative to horizon.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Trend regimes dominate: shorting strength in a persistent uptrend produces repeated small losses and occasional large ones (negative skew), so Sharpe is strongly negative even if hit rate looks acceptable; or the volatility filter makes the sample too small and unstable.
hypotheses.hypothesis: After a large sustained multi-day advance accompanied by elevated realised volatility, perpetual long positioning becomes crowded and funding turns expensive, so marginal buyers are financed rather than convicted; the resulting overhang means downside air-pockets are deeper than upside continuation. Unlike the earlier impulse-fade attempts, which faded 5-30 minute overshoots and were destroyed by cost, this fades a slow-built positioning extreme and holds 4 hours, giving the reversion room to exceed the 10 bp hurdle. The short-only construction exploits the structural asymmetry (leverage is long-biased) instead of assuming symmetry.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Low-volatility drift is exactly the regime where 10 bps is large relative to available movement, so even a correct directional call earns too little; alternatively compression resolves against the prior drift (mean reversion inside the range) and the strategy systematically buys the top of quiet ranges.
hypotheses.hypothesis: When realised volatility over the last 12 hours is unusually low, market makers quote tight and inventory sits close to flat; a price that has nonetheless drifted above its 4-hour mean in that quiet state indicates one-sided accumulation absorbing thin liquidity, and the subsequent volatility normalisation tends to resolve in the direction of that accumulation. The earlier range-expansion breakout failed because it entered after expansion had already happened (buying the widest bar, paying the worst spread); here entry is before expansion, in the compressed state, with a 4-hour hold to capture the expansion leg.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Boundary flow is real but is fully absorbed within one or two bars by liquidity providers who anticipate it, so signed forward returns over 24 bars are indistinguishable from zero and the strategy nets roughly minus the cost; or the flow is direction-neutral so the 'both' construction averages to nothing.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Scheduled activity clusters at the top of the hour: funding accruals, TWAP/VWAP slice boundaries, systematic hedge rebalances and index-linked flows all restart there, and that mechanical flow tends to extend whatever direction the preceding hour established. My earlier clock attempt was rejected for zero trades because the market conditions were stacked with persistence on top of the phase gate; here the gate is a single lenient one-hour trend condition evaluated only at phase 0 of each 60-bar hour, side both, so the rule fires often enough to be measurable, with a 2-hour hold to let the boundary flow play out.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Low participation also means low realised movement, so gross per-trade return stays under the 10 bp hurdle; and volume droughts are frequently followed by a volume burst in the opposite direction (the drift was thin-liquidity noise), turning the tail of the distribution against the position.
hypotheses.hypothesis: When traded volume is persistently below its own 8-hour norm, resting depth is thin and there is little contrarian liquidity to absorb directional order flow, so an existing multi-hour uptrend can extend on very little size (a liquidity-drought drift). This differs from the earlier quiet-trend attempt, which conditioned on volatility and traded a short trend window with persistence gating; here the conditioning variable is participation (volume_z) rather than volatility, the trend window is 8 hours, and the hold is 4 hours so a single decision covers many bars of drift instead of churning.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Liquidation cascades terminate within a few bars and are followed by a sharp mechanical rebound as makers reload, so a 24-bar hold gives back the initial move; also entries occur at the worst possible liquidity (widest effective spread), meaning realised cost exceeds the assumed 10 bps and net stays negative.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Downside volume shocks in perpetuals are mechanically different from upside ones: forced liquidations of long leverage generate market sell orders that push price into further liquidation clusters, so a sharp one-hour decline confirmed by an extreme volume spike marks the start of a queue of forced sellers rather than a completed flush. My earlier volume-shock work faded these events symmetrically and lost, which is direct evidence that absorption is not the dominant mechanism at this timescale; this proposal takes the same event class but goes with the flow, short-only, and extends the hold to 2 hours so the cascade tail rather than the first bounce is harvested.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: In a persistently declining regime the 288-bar discount is itself the trend signal, so buying it means fighting genuine information flow: entries cluster inside continuing downtrends and the 48-bar hold accumulates negative drift, producing gross losses larger than the cost saving from low turnover.
hypotheses.hypothesis: After a multi-day drawdown (price well below its 288-bar mean) that is accompanied by elevated participation, forced sellers and de-risking flow have transferred inventory to liquidity providers who are structurally short-gamma in cash terms; they must buy back / re-hedge, and passive bid-side rebuilding produces a slow multi-hour upward drift. Unlike my earlier short-horizon fades (H1, H5, H6) which each earned roughly zero gross, the horizon here is deliberately long (288-bar signal, 48-bar hold) so that the expected move magnitude is several tenths of a percent rather than a few basis points, giving room over the 10 bps round trip.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Cross-horizon agreement is a lagging condition: by the time both the 144-bar trend and the 24-bar slope are positive, the execution programme is largely complete, so entries land near local highs and the 48-bar hold gives back the drift, leaving gross near zero and net near minus cost.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Large directional participants split orders over many hours (TWAP/VWAP style), so genuine institutional accumulation shows up as agreement between a slow half-day trend and a still-positive shorter moving-average slope. Requiring two timescales to agree filters out the single-horizon trend noise that killed H2 and H7 (where one trend condition admitted many false starts), and the 48-bar hold matches the multi-hour execution schedule so the captured drift can exceed 10 bps.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Boundary flow is mechanical and two-sided (both buy and sell programmes complete on the same bar), so the conditional drift after the boundary is symmetric noise; with only a 12-bar hold the average move is well under 10 bps and the strategy dies purely on cost.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Scheduled execution and systematic signal evaluation cluster on hour boundaries; the final 5-minute bar of an hour concentrates slice-completion and hourly-candle-close order flow, so a move already in progress into that bar tends to be extended by boundary-aligned participants. My earlier clock attempts (H3, H10) were rejected for producing zero trades because the phase constraint was stacked with several market filters; here the rule is deliberately minimal (one return condition plus phase) so the sample is large enough to falsify.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Low realised volatility often precedes regime change, so a sharp move out of compression is exactly the breakout case: shorting it means standing in front of a new volatility regime, and a handful of large adverse holds will overwhelm many small mean-reverting wins.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Inside a structurally quiet volatility regime, resting stop and liquidation clusters sit close to price; a fast half-hour advance in such a regime is usually a stop-run through thin resting depth rather than information arrival, and once the stop cluster is consumed the book refills and price retraces toward the pre-run level. This differs from H5, which faded impulses measured by a volatility shock (i.e. inside already-turbulent tape where impulses are information-driven); conditioning on a LOW long-window volatility isolates the mechanically driven subset.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: High volatility is symmetric in practice: violent upside squeezes of short inventory occur in exactly the same regime, so the conditional mean is near zero while the variance is huge, giving a poor Sharpe and net loss equal to cost; alternatively the state is so common that trades re-open continuously and turnover destroys the edge.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Perpetual futures carry crowded leveraged long inventory; when realised volatility is high, margin requirements and risk limits bind on the long side far more than on the short side, so high-volatility regimes carry a persistent negative conditional drift (deleveraging pressure) independent of any specific impulse. Rather than trading a single cascade event as H12 did, this is a regime-state short with a long hold, so the position collects the whole unwind drift instead of one 30-minute impulse, and requiring the state to persist several bars avoids single-bar volatility spikes.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Trend termination is exactly when pullbacks stop being bought; the rule will systematically buy the first leg of every trend reversal, so a minority of large adverse 24-bar holds cancels the many small resumption gains and leaves net below cost.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Within an established multi-day uptrend, short-term pullbacks are typically inventory-driven: market makers who are short into the trend buy back, and systematic trend followers add on retracements, so a one-hour dip against a positive 288-bar trend is followed by resumption. The mechanism combines a short-horizon reversal with a long-horizon continuation, which none of my previous plans did (they either faded moves outright or chased trend at the same horizon), and entering on weakness rather than strength improves the entry price by more than the 10 bps cost if the trend premise holds.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Most likely killer: 'calm after a daily decline' is simply the middle of a persistent downtrend with low realised vol, so the position bleeds with the drift and the 48-bar hold multiplies the loss (this is how H7 lost 23bps). Secondary killer: the joint condition is rare enough that trade count collapses below the minimum, or the reversion completes inside the first few bars and the remaining hold gives back the gain.
hypotheses.hypothesis: After a full-day decline (return over 288 bars strongly negative) the reversion trade only pays once forced selling has actually stopped. Requiring current short-horizon volatility to be LOW (volatility(24) compressed) is the structural filter my earlier capitulation-reversion attempt (H13) lacked: H13 bought while the liquidation flow was still hitting the book, so entries were filled into ongoing supply and gross edge was only ~+1bps. Here the mechanism is inventory rebalancing by market makers and passive bid replenishment AFTER the impulse decays: dealers who absorbed the down-move are short-inventory versus their target and lean their quotes upward, producing slow upward drift over the next several hours. A 48-bar hold amortises the 10bps round trip over 4 hours, which is the only horizon over which such a slow inventory-unwind drift can exceed cost.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: High volume in an extended uptrend is more likely to mark the distribution/exhaustion point where the slicing is finishing, so entries land at local highs and the 48-bar hold rides the give-back. Alternatively the volume_z condition mostly fires on single-bar shocks whose displacement is already complete at the fill on the next open, leaving gross edge near zero and net near minus cost.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Trend continuation without flow confirmation failed twice (H2 quiet-trend persistence, H11 low-participation drift): in thin books an existing trend is mostly stale drift already in the price, so there is no residual order flow to push it further. The mechanism I now test is participation-confirmed accumulation: a multi-hour uptrend (trend(96) above its SMA by a clear margin) that is accompanied by ELEVATED volume relative to the same window (volume_z(96) > 1) indicates real size being worked through the book rather than passive drift, and large orders are typically sliced over many hours, so unfilled residual demand keeps arriving. That residual demand is the only mechanism that can pay more than 10bps over a 4-hour hold.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Volatility compression is the classic pre-expansion state, so a meaningful minority of entries will be followed by a downside expansion that is large enough to wipe out many small gains; sharpe collapses even if hit-rate is above 50%. Also the two conditions are highly persistent, so consecutive re-entries turn this into near-continuous exposure whose cost per unit of drift is still above the drift itself.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Regime-level rather than event-level mechanism, which none of my prior proposals tested: when realised volatility over a long window (96 bars) is compressed, leveraged participants face low margin utilisation, market makers quote tighter, and the marginal flow is dominated by patient passive accumulation rather than forced liquidation. In such regimes the drift term dominates the noise term, so a slowly rising long-window moving average (ma_slope(288) positive) should extend with high hit-rate and small drawdown. The edge is not an impulse to be captured but a low-noise carry: the Sharpe comes from many small positive 4-hour holds, and with 48-bar holds the 10bps cost is paid once per 4 hours of exposure.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: If the boundary push is information-driven rather than schedule-driven, the fade is run over and the short loses on continuation; alternatively the retracement is only a few bps — smaller than the 10bps round trip — because market makers already price the periodic imbalance, leaving net around minus cost like H15. The clock may also cut trade count enough to make results statistically empty.
hypotheses.hypothesis: My two clock-momentum attempts were rejected for zero trades (over-constrained) and the hour-close momentum version lost cost (H15), which is evidence that boundary flow is NOT informative continuation. The mechanism I test now is the opposite and is mechanically motivated: scheduled execution programmes and periodic hedging are concentrated into the final minutes of an hour, mechanically displacing price beyond fair value with impatient taker flow; once the schedule resets at the boundary the pressure disappears and the displacement retraces. So I fade an up-push that is (a) fast (return over 6 bars clearly positive), (b) taker-driven (volume_z(24) elevated), and (c) observed exactly at the hour boundary, holding 12 bars for the retracement. hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: High-volatility declines are also where the sharpest short-squeeze rallies occur; a handful of violent upward reversals inside the 48-bar hold can erase the accumulated drift and produce a negative Sharpe even with a positive median trade. hypotheses.hypothesis: H17 (high-vol short drift) produced zero trades because the volatility and trend thresholds were jointly too extreme; H12 shorted single-bar cascades whose displacement was already spent by the next open. That produces a multi-hour, not multi-minute, downward drift. So I use a long-window trend condition (trend(144) below its mean) as the regime definer, a moderate volatility(48) floor as the stress condition, and a 48-bar hold to capture drift rather than impulse.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: The obvious killer is that a dip large enough to matter is precisely the dip that breaks the trend — a genuine regime change — so I buy the first leg of a reversal and hold it for two hours. Second killer: the snap-back happens within the very first bar after the signal, so the fill at the next open already gives away the entire edge and net collapses to minus cost again.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Buying pullbacks inside an uptrend was my least-bad result (H18: gross roughly +1bps), which suggests the reversion mechanism is real but the displacement I demanded was too small to clear a 10bps round trip. The mechanism is a liquidity vacuum: a fast multi-bar drop (return over 6 bars deeply negative) inside an intact multi-hour uptrend (trend(144) clearly positive) is stop-cascade and market-maker-inventory driven, not information driven; resting bids that were pulled during the sweep are replaced within tens of minutes and price snaps back toward the trend anchor. This version demands a materially larger displacement so the expected snap-back is several times the previous attempt's, and extends the hold to 24 bars so the full replenishment, not just the first bounce bar, is captured.

The mechanism that would produce this is perpetual-swap crowding: sustained multi-day drift attracts leveraged directional flow that pushes the perp above/below fair value, and funding payments plus periodic deleveraging pull it back. Therefore taking the OPPOSITE side of a stretched 24-hour deviation from its own moving average, held for four hours, should capture that give-back. Falsifiable claim: entering counter to trend(288) extremes with a 48-bar hold produces positive net bps per trade.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Volume drought is likely to cluster in structurally quiet periods where realised 4-hour moves are small in both directions, so the average absolute payoff shrinks below the cost hurdle even if the sign is right; or the drought persists and price simply grinds lower on thin liquidity.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Previous drawdown-reversion attempts (H13, H19) triggered on price alone and traded thousands of times, earning roughly +1 bp gross - too thin for costs. The sharper mechanism is participation collapse: after a sustained multi-hour decline, forced and discretionary sellers finish, and the tell is that traded volume falls far below its own long-run mean while price is still depressed. With no seller left and passive bids replenished, the path of least resistance is upward drift. Making volume drought (not price) the trigger should select far fewer, higher-payoff events. hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Quiet-regime dislocations are precisely the cases where the 4-hour forward move is tiny, so a correct sign can still produce sub-10 bps capture; and a subset of these drops are the leading edge of a genuine regime shift, whose losses are large enough to swamp many small wins.
hypotheses.hypothesis: H16 faded low-volatility stop runs and came closest to breakeven on a gross basis (-9.5 net, i.e. ~+0.5 gross) but with only 261 trades and, evidently, too short a capture window. This proposal keeps the quiet-regime conditioning but extends the capture horizon to 48 bars so the full inventory unwind, not just the first bounce, is harvested. Falsifiable claim: long after a sharp 1-hour drop inside a low-volatility 24-hour regime, held 4 hours, nets above cost.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Volume spikes in downtrends may equally mark capitulation lows where the squeeze becomes a durable regime turn, so the short is entered exactly at the bottom; also the spike condition does not verify the impulse was upward, so a fraction of entries short into an already-completed flush and pay the mean-reversion bounce.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Neither plain bear-regime drift (H23) nor plain volume shocks (H1) worked, but their conjunction describes a specific mechanism not yet tested: inside an established multi-day downtrend, a high-volume upward impulse is mechanically a short squeeze - shorts being stopped or liquidated - not new demand. Once the forced buying is complete the order book has no follow-through bid, so price returns to the prevailing downtrend. The volume-z spike identifies the forced component, and the long-horizon negative trend identifies the regime that reasserts itself. Falsifiable claim: shorting after volume_z(48) spikes above 2 while trend(288) is negative, held 48 bars, nets above cost.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: High volatility with a rising price is also the signature of a genuine repricing (short squeeze into a new range), where continuation dominates; the short then absorbs fat right-tail losses. Even if the mean sign is negative, volatility-conditioned shorts historically fail on variance rather than mean, so Sharpe stays negative.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Rallies differ in quality: one that advances while realised volatility is rising is being driven by leveraged momentum chasers whose positions are margin-sensitive, whereas a rally on falling volatility reflects genuine absorption. Prior exhaustion tests (H8, H23) conditioned on positioning proxies or regime alone and never on the volatility/price divergence itself. The claim here is that a positive 8-hour trend co-existing with elevated 4-hour volatility marks an unstable, over-leveraged advance whose 4-hour forward return is negative because the marginal buyer is already fully levered. Falsifiable claim: shorting when volatility(48) is high and trend(96) is positive, held 48 bars, nets above the 10 bps hurdle.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Persistence filters usually delay entry until the impact is already priced, so the fade captures only the residual decay, which may be smaller than costs; and if the signal state is sticky the position is held through genuine information-driven trends, producing large adverse excursions on both sides.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Every prior plan used a fixed holding window, which forces exits on a clock regardless of whether the pressure driving the trade is still present. This proposal instead detects the footprint of a working execution algorithm - a 30-minute return that stays beyond a threshold for three consecutive bars, i.e. persistent one-directional taker aggression rather than a single print - and takes the other side, staying in position only while that footprint is live. Mechanism: parent orders sliced by VWAP/TWAP engines pay the spread repeatedly and push price away from fair value; when the slice ends the temporary impact decays, so the counter-position is closed exactly as the pressure disappears rather than at an arbitrary bar count. Falsifiable claim: state-exited fades of persistent directional thrust net more than 10 bps per round trip.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: The sharp drop is the first leg of a multi-hour cascade rather than an overshoot: in stressed regimes downside momentum autocorrelates, so buying the 2-hour drop and holding 4 hours captures the second leg down and loses several multiples of the 10 bps cost on a minority of trades, dragging mean net bps negative even if the median trade is profitable.
hypotheses.hypothesis: When a sharp 2-hour decline (return(24) <= -0.5%) occurs inside a regime whose multi-day realised volatility is already elevated, the marginal seller is usually a margin-constrained or stop-driven account, and resting bid liquidity has been thinned. Market makers who absorb that flow are compensated by a wide reversion premium, but the premium is only paid out over hours, not minutes. Earlier capitulation-reversion attempts (H13, H19) were killed by holding the position far too short relative to the amplitude of the dislocation, so a ~1 bp gross edge was swamped by the 10 bps round trip. This version demands a genuinely stressed background regime (volatility(288) high) and holds a full 48 bars (4 hours) so that inventory-rebalancing drift has time to exceed cost.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Deviation from the 8-hour mean is itself a trend proxy, so in any sustained trending block both mirrored branches fight the drift and the loss on trend days exceeds the small mean-reversion gains in range days; the unconditional both-sided form has no regime filter (budget forbids one) to switch itself off.
hypotheses.hypothesis: In the absence of a directional flow imbalance, price oscillates around the value area set by market-maker inventory: deviations of the close from its own 8-hour moving average (trend(96)) are mostly the footprint of transient taker imbalance and decay as inventory is worked off. Trading only large deviations (|trend(96)| >= ~0.4%) makes the signal rare, and mirroring it on both sides keeps the rule symmetric so no directional regime assumption is needed. Unlike H25 and H27, the deviation horizon (96 bars) and the hold (48 bars) are matched, so the trade is given the same timescale the mechanism operates on instead of being closed inside the noise band.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Most extreme volume prints in perpetual futures are liquidation or de-risking events regardless of trend context, so entries cluster immediately before continued two-sided violence; realised follow-through is symmetric and the long-only version pays cost on a coin flip.
hypotheses.hypothesis: A very large volume print (volume_z(96) >= ~2.5) that occurs while price is still above its multi-day mean is more likely to be a size-driven participant working an order into available liquidity than a forced liquidation, because liquidations of longs would have broken structure to the downside. Such absorption events mark where an informed buyer is willing to pay for immediacy, and the remainder of the order plus follow-on flow produces continuation over the next hours. This is deliberately the opposite of H1 (which faded volume shocks and lost) and is conditioned on structural context, addressing H1's failure that unconditional volume-shock fades trade against informed size.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Low volume during an extension is often just a quiet grind higher in which liquidity providers keep raising quotes; shorting it means fighting slow persistent drift, so the strategy bleeds a little on many trades and gets hurt badly whenever the quiet extension accelerates into a squeeze.
hypotheses.hypothesis: An extension of price well above its multi-day mean (trend(288) >= ~0.5%) that is accompanied by below-average participation (volume_z(288) < 0.5) is carried by leveraged positioning rather than by new spot demand or hedging flow. Financing costs on that positioning accrue continuously, and thin participation means little real demand to defend the level, so the extension unwinds. Requiring the divergence to persist for 6 consecutive bars filters out one-bar volume artefacts, which is the flaw I attribute to H6: it fired thousands of times on transient single-bar divergences at short horizons and paid cost on noise.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Recoveries out of depressed structure are exactly where the sharpest upside impulses occur (short squeezes, basis re-normalisation), so a short-only rule collects small wins and occasional very large losses; the tail dominates and net bps per trade stays below the 10 bps cost hurdle.
hypotheses.hypothesis: When price sits below its multi-day mean (trend(288) <= -0.5%) but has rallied ~0.4% or more over the last 4 hours, the rally is typically short-covering and dip-buying into an inventory position that dealers and trend followers still want to be short of; supply above is refreshed as the bounce approaches prior distribution levels. The mechanism is asymmetric to the bear structure, so it should be traded short-only and held long enough (48 bars) for supply to reassert. H28 tried a related idea but was parameterised so tightly it produced one trade; here both conditions are set at magnitudes that should fire often enough to be measurable while still being selective.

hypotheses.expected_failure_mode: Volatility clusters: high short-horizon vol against a calm background predicts more vol, not direction, so the long bias is unfounded and the position is effectively random with a 10 bps toll; alternatively the entries concentrate in a handful of episodes, giving too few effective independent observations for any measured edge to survive.
hypotheses.hypothesis: Use volatility term structure alone, with no price-return condition, as the entry: a 4-hour realised volatility that is high (>= ~0.4% per 5m bar) while the multi-day background volatility is still calm (< ~0.2%) identifies a fresh de-leveraging shock in an otherwise orderly regime. In leveraged perpetual markets such isolated shocks are predominantly downside-initiated (long liquidations, stop cascades), so an unconditional long taken on the volatility signature harvests the asymmetric bounce without needing to specify the price path, avoiding the selection bias of return-threshold triggers that also catch orderly declines. Every prior shock hypothesis (H5, H9, H12) keyed on price or range; none tested the volatility ratio as the sole trigger.
